newsitem.title: PERU: Peru army says captures 38 MRTA rebels in jungle.
newsitem.headline: Peru army says captures 38 MRTA rebels in jungle.

text.p: The Peruvian military said on Tuesday it has captured 38 jungle members of the Marxist rebel movement holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima for 91 days.

The army also seized 10 rifles and 11 grenades in a sweep through Peru's central jungle, the only area where the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) has a permanent armed presence, the Armed Forces Joint Command said in a statement.
The captured group of "MRTA terrorists" had planned to attack late February an army base in the town of Oxapampa, some 200 miles (325 kms) east of Lima, the statement said.
The army did not say when the suspected rebels were detained, but local media has reported several captures over the last few weeks.
As late as Sunday, however, the MRTA said none of its members had been captured despite a major army offensive to flush them out of their jungle strongholds.

Comrade Alejandro, who identified himself as a member of the MRTA's high-command, told Reuters in a communication from the jungle, the army was deploying more than 500 soldiers to search for the group's military bases in the provinces of Oxapampa and Chanchamayo.
The senior rebel claimed the army had only detained villagers in the region and alleged they were MRTA members.

A leading Peruvian human rights group, APRODEH, also said last week the whereabouts of four villagers in the area were still unknown after an army operation March 9 led to the detention of 21 peasants.
Villagers in the area told local TV station America Television on Tuesday the army had killed one person and tortured others in the army operation.
"They threw him, pulled him and he probably tried to escape and the (bullet) caught him," said Florencia Roldan, who said her husband Fortunato Chipana was shot dead by soldiers on Feb. 25.
The joint-forces, which had earlier denied the sweep, said the army had respected human rights in its operation.

The army operation comes as a top envoy from Tokyo visited Lima in a bid to curb Peru's hawkish tendencies. In a two-hour meeting at Government palace Japan's Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura urged President Alberto Fujimori to move faster on talks to free the 72 hostages.
With negotiations between Peru and the rebels making scant progress, speculation has grown that Fujimori may tire of talking and try to storm the mined and booby-trapped diplomatic compound.
"Mr. Komura expressed his desire for the discussions ... to be accelerated," Katsuyuki Tanaka, deputy director of Japan's special office in Lima, told reporters.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday morning, Komura said he asked Fujimori to respond to proposals by a three-man mediation panel, known as the guarantors commission, to resolve the 91-day standoff peacefully. He did not say what those proposals were.
"I asked President Fujimori to respond to efforts by the guarantors commission," Komura said through a translator.

The main reason for Komura's three-nation visit to Latin America was to arrange for asylum in Cuba and the Dominican Republic for all or some of the rebels in exchange for handing over the hostages unharmed, the diplomat said.
Fujimori went to Cuba last month to arrange an asylum deal with Cuban leader Fidel Castro.

Komura, who is due to leave Lima on Wednesday afternoon for Havana, also handed Fujimori a letter from Hashimoto asking him to redouble efforts to solve the standoff peacefully, local radio reports said.
